intro: A lullaby in E minor turns to E major and back again. Repeated B’s keep the piano gently rocking, even when the music seems too drowsy to finish.

sections.label: A · Repeated B’s in E minor
A′ · The E-minor lullaby returns
sections.mNote: A final ritardando leads to a suspended ending

cues.title: A B that keeps rocking
cues.text: B pulses in the middle of the piano while the upper notes rock above it. The left hand has the same dotted lilt. Schumann keeps the E-minor lullaby quiet, repeating the little figures as if the child is nearly asleep.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, plate 6016, p. 18, opening eight bars: piano, repeated B’s and dotted figures in both hands. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/f/fe/IMSLP03060-Schumann-Op015Brt6016.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The lullaby turns to major
cues.text: E major warms the middle passage, marked pianissimo. The rocking continues underneath a fuller right-hand melody. As the phrase descends, the right hand moves into the bass clef, close to the left.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 18, third and fourth systems: E-major signature, pianissimo, descending melody and right-hand bass-clef changes.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Sleep overtakes the phrase
cues.text: The E-minor opening returns, with its repeated B and rocking accompaniment. In the last phrase Schumann stretches a ritardando across several bars. The hands finally stop on a chord held under a fermata, leaving the lullaby hanging.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 19, final two systems: return to the one-sharp signature, piano, final ritardando and fermata.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: E minor turns to E major
transitions.from: A · Repeated B’s in E minor
transitions.how: At the double bar, E minor turns directly to E major and the dynamic falls to pianissimo. The left hand keeps rocking on E while the right hand opens into fuller chords. The new G♯ changes the light.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 18, second to third systems: change to E major, pianissimo and continued E bass.

transitions.title: The minor-key rocking returns
transitions.how: A ritardando slows the middle passage. The key signature returns to one sharp, and the familiar B pulses above E-minor harmony. Schumann marks the return piano; the left hand resumes the opening rocking figure.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 19, second to third systems: ritardando, return to E minor and piano.

composer.epithet: A bookseller’s son who put lovers, masks and arguments into piano music, and made criticism a form of friendship.
facts: Friedrich Wieck, piano; Heinrich Dorn, composition
Co-founded the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik in 1834; edited it until 1844
Married Clara Wieck in 1840; eight children, seven surviving infancy
composer.background:
Robert Schumann grew up among books in Zwickau. His father August sold and published them, and encouraged his son’s music; Robert read Jean Paul’s novels while learning the piano. The books offered twins, disguises, conversations that wandered away from their subject and returned by an unexpected door. In Papillons, his early set of piano dances, Schumann took up the masked ball at the end of Jean Paul’s Flegeljahre. The music changes partners every few bars.

He went to Leipzig to study law in 1828, moved to Heidelberg the following year, and finally persuaded his mother to let him pursue music. Friedrich Wieck undertook to train him as a pianist. Wieck’s young daughter Clara was already performing in public; Robert was the older pupil who had much to catch up on. By 1832, paralysis in his right hand had ended his hopes of becoming a virtuoso. He studied composition with Heinrich Dorn and began building a life at the writing desk.
